name: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
title: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
answer: Mapping financial AI to the rules is the work of connecting each model, tool or automated decision in a finance function to the specific regulation, accounting standard or supervisory expectation that governs it. It covers credit scoring, fraud detection, anti money laundering checks, algorithmic trading, automated advice and back office automation, and it reaches across accounting, prudential and conduct rules at once. The output is usually a register or control matrix that shows, for each use of AI, which obligation applies, who owns it and what evidence shows it is met.

sections.body: Mapping financial AI to the rules is the work of connecting each model, tool or automated decision in a finance function to the specific regulation, accounting standard or supervisory expectation that governs it. It covers credit scoring, fraud detection, anti money laundering checks, algorithmic trading, automated advice and back office automation, and it reaches across accounting, prudential and conduct rules at once. The output is usually a register or control matrix that shows, for each use of AI, which obligation applies, who owns it and what evidence shows it is met.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a combination of the firm's own systems of record, such as the general ledger, the trading platform and the customer database, and a governance layer that holds the model inventory, the control library and the mapping between them. Registers are often kept in spreadsheets or in governance, risk and compliance platforms, with model documentation stored alongside. Because the rules change, the mapping has to be refreshed against regulatory sources, and this site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages as one view of how much ground that covers.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start from the obligation and work down, or from the model and work up, and the two directions have to meet. A typical pass identifies the AI use case, classifies its risk and materiality, traces the data it consumes and produces, and then attaches the relevant rule, control and test. Accountants and risk staff do much of this by reading the rule text and interviewing the model owner, then recording the conclusion with a date and a named reviewer. The mapping is only useful if it can be re performed when the model, the data or the rule changes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on accountability, explainability and the provenance of data and decisions. A firm needs to show who approved a model, what it was allowed to do, what data trained and feeds it, and how a customer or auditor can get a plain account of a decision that affected them. Records must be retained and traceable, and personal or confidential financial data must be handled under the applicable privacy and security rules. Where a model is bought rather than built, the contract and the vendor's documentation become part of the evidence, and gaps there are a common finding.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous mapping rather than an annual exercise, with rule changes, model changes and control tests feeding the same register. Supervisors increasingly expect firms to demonstrate that AI use is identified, assessed and monitored, not merely documented once. That pushes the work closer to real time, and it raises the value of shared taxonomies that let a single control satisfy several obligations at once. The open question is how quickly the mapping can keep pace with both the rules and the models.
